forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bromley forecasts a £62.4m schools grant deficit at year end, with a £36.0m high needs grant confirmed
news_drafts.lead:
Bromley's Executive has been told the council expects a deficit of £62.403m on its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, at the end of 2026/27. The November budget monitoring report projects an overspend of £22.339m on the grant during the year, added to £39.979m carried forward from 2025/26. Officers are preparing a recovery plan with the Department for Education, which the paper says will be considered in due course.

The government has confirmed a High Needs Stability Grant for Bromley of £35.981m. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The grant covers 90% of the cumulative DSG deficit to 2025/26, and the paper says it is intended to offset historic DSG deficits. The council expects about £36m to be received in 2026/27. Its updated forecast assumes the same 90% proportion for 2026/27 and 2027/28.

The report also sets out the drawdown from reserves needed to balance the 2026/27 budget. It says the estimated drawdown increases from £25.422m to £33.181m. A further drawdown of £2.3m, bringing the total to £35.481m, would be needed to meet the balance remaining after the High Needs Stability Grant.

news_drafts.headline: Bromley's risk register lists uncertain government support for schools deficit from 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Bromley Council's finance risk register records uncertainty over how much government support it will receive from 2026/27 towards a deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, where a deficit is usually an overspend on support for children with special needs. The register is Appendix D to papers for the Executive, Resources and Contracts Policy Development and Scrutiny Committee, which meets on 23 November 2026.

The register lists the uncertainty as a cause of its risk on government reforms and new burdens. It describes the position as "Uncertainty on level of Government support for DSG deficit from 2026/27 (90% was funded up to 2025/26)".

The register gives that risk a current rating of 12 and a target rating of 9. Both are scored as likelihood multiplied by impact. The papers do not give a figure for the deficit.

news_drafts.headline: Bromley forecasts £22.4m high-needs overspend for 2026/27; 90% SEND deficit write-off awaited
news_drafts.lead:
Bromley Council forecasts a £22.4m overspend for 2026/27 on its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, according to papers for the Children, Education and Families committee on 18 November. The overspend is mainly in high needs, the part that funds special educational needs and disabilities. The papers also say a government write-off of 90% of historic SEND deficits would, on current figures, remove £36.0m of Bromley's deficit and leave £4.0m at the end of 2025/26.

The write-off depends on a "local SEND reform plan", which Bromley submitted to the Department for Education in June 2026. The paper says the allocation, and any drawdown in November 2026, are still awaited. The council carried forward a DSG deficit of £40.0m from 2025/26 and estimates its DSG reserve at £62.3m by the end of 2026/27. Of this year's amount, £16.5m is already budgeted. The paper identifies a further £5.8m that it says will be met from reserves unless ongoing funding is found, and it says the specific reserves have not yet been identified. It describes the position as "financially unsustainable" in the medium to longer term. Education, health and care plans numbered 5,070 in September 2026, 46 above the budget profile of 5,024, against 27 above in April.

On SEND transport, the risk register says independent travel training and personal transport budgets are "successfully driving down costs". The committee approved in June 2026 a procurement through an Open Framework, with the contract starting in September 2027.

findings.headline: Parking proposals projected to add £633,958 of income in 2027/28 and £663,958 in 2028/29, against a £40,000 implementation cost
findings.detail: The summary table gives the income for each proposal by year. The paper states that implementation costs of £40,000 will be met from existing revenue budgets and offset by the additional income. It also states an ongoing annual saving of £174,000 after inflation, which it does not reconcile to the table in the text.
findings.matters: A total income and saving figure that a council presents as a sustainability measure, with the basis of the saving left unexplained, is one a peer finance officer may want to test.
findings.quote: These proposals will deliver an ongoing annual saving of £174,000, after allowing for

findings.headline: Wharton Road closure costs to go through a capital project business case to avoid a revenue pressure once the site is no longer operational
findings.detail: The property section says that Wharton Road is currently an operational car park under the APCOA management contract. Once an alternative use is agreed, day-to-day management will move to the delivery team. Any associated costs will form part of a capital project business case, so they do not become a revenue pressure.
findings.matters: Routing the costs of a site's change of use through capital rather than revenue is a treatment finance directors and lenders will want to see explicitly.
findings.quote: Any associated costs will form part of the business case for approval of a capital project to avoid a revenue pressure

findings.headline: New paid parking bays around railway stations projected to add £0 in 2027/28, £30,000 in 2028/29 and £91,000 in 2029/30
findings.detail: The paper proposes a minimum tariff of 50p per hour, with maximum daily charges from £0.80 to £7.00, at up to 20 stations. Officers are to run feasibility studies over 12 to 18 months. The paper says approval does not mean all listed locations will be implemented, and that consultation responses and objections must be considered first.
findings.matters: Income from a new charging scheme that is phased over three years and conditional on feasibility and consultation is a projection other councils can compare with their own charging plans.
findings.quote: The introduction of new paid parking bays around railway stations is likely to generate an ongoing income to the Council

findings.headline: Executive asked to agree in principle to closing Wharton Road car park, with a projected saving of £4,758 a year
findings.detail: The paper describes the car park as loss-making. It says the saving reflects removal of maintenance, enforcement and business rates costs, which currently outweigh its income. It also says 'the Council is experiencing significant financial pressures across its services', and that closure is subject to legal processes and equality impact consideration. Officers are asked to progress 22 potential additional permit bays to replace the 16 that would be lost.
findings.matters: Closing a site that the paper calls loss-making, to free land for redevelopment, is a specific asset decision that other councils reviewing their car park estates would recognise.
findings.figures: £4,758 (annual saving, 2027/28 and 2028/29); 22 potential permit bays; 16 bays lost
findings.quote: The projected annual saving of £4,758 from the closure of Wharton Road Car Park

findings.headline: Resident, business and visitor permit charges proposed to rise 26%, projected at £148,200 in 2027/28
findings.detail: The paper says permit charges have been unchanged since April 2023. It states that increased contract costs for the permit management system and for enforcing Controlled Parking Zones can no longer be accommodated within existing fee levels, so a 26% increase is proposed.
findings.matters: A fee increase set against a stated inability to absorb contract costs within existing charges shows how a council is passing service cost rises to users.
findings.quote: Permit charges have remained unchanged since April 2023.

daily_post.headline: Experts at Hand grant is being used to offset part of the staffing overspend.
daily_post.lead: Grant-funded offset of staffing pressures is a temporary fix that a finance director at another council would want to track against the grant's end date.
